#17150. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2087 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less.
  • Recent findings suggest that it should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

According to recent reports, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

Recent findings suggest that it should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching new lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

It has been revealed that getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

It has been revealed that if you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

When you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your manufacturer can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

Industry observers note that if you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

It has been revealed that I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a newly introduced branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

In a recent development, in the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

As the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for stated Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Industry observers note that not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the significant chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

What I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing fresh folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a new piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

It has been revealed that while I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While GTA 6 has been receiving unbelievable praise and is technically considered one of the best video games of all time according to Metacritic, that certainly doesn't mean it's immune to criticism.

In a recent development, one of the big talking points both before and after launch has been that it's a 30FPS experience across all Xbox and PlayStation consoles, and if you're going from 60FPS back to 30FPS, there's definitely an adjustment period. Some people are absolutely fine with that, while others are finding it extremely difficult to go back.

For what it's worth, our friends at Digital Foundry have been analysing this in depth today:.

Rockstar Games has already confirmed recently that even the PS5 Pro doesn't come close to running GTA 6 at 60FPS due to the system's processor not being powerful enough, so we might be forced to wait until the next generation of consoles (and PC) before the game will become playable at 60 frames per-second.

"The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game’s visual fidelity. While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates.”.

With all of this in mind, we're interested to hear what you think about playing games at 30FPS on Xbox, PlayStation or anywhere else. It's becoming much more common that 60FPS is the default these days, but there are still some phenomenal 30FPS-only experiences out there, and it's a shame to think people are missing out on them.

I personally much prefer playing at 60FPS if I can, and there are certain games I will avoid at 30FPS until they get a patch down the line (like Mafia: Definitive Edition), but when it comes to industry-defining masterpieces like Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto VI, the last thing I'd want is for them to scale back the detail in order to squeeze in a 60FPS mode.

Industry observers note that so, what do you think? Tell us in the poll above and in the comments section below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

videogame executive Peter Moore, known for his time at Sega, Xbox, and Electronic Arts as well as a couple of famous tattoos, has expressed hope that the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 will provide a much-needed "shot in the arm" for the videogame industry.

Moore began with a faked photo of himself rolling up his sleeve to reveal a GTA 6 tattoo—although the photo is based on his real-world tattoo-based reveal of Grand Theft Auto 4 on Xbox 360 at E3 2006.

Industry observers note that "In all seriousness, the videogame industry could really use a moment like this," Moore wrote on X after posting the image. "We've been through a challenging period. Studio closures, redundancies, cancelled projects and enormous uncertainty have taken their toll on an industry that has given so much to so many, myself included.

"That's why the launch of GTA 6 feels so significant. It's more than the release of a hugely anticipated game. It's an opportunity to remind the world of the extraordinary power of this industry to create, innovate, entertain and bring people together.".

Sources indicate that moore's career in the game industry began at Sega, where he oversaw the launch of the Dreamcast and promptly rose to become president and chief operating officer of Sega of America. In 2003 he went to Microsoft and became its Corporate Vice President of Interactive Entertainment Business, Entertainment and Devices Division, heading up its Xbox division; in 2007 he joined EA Sports, and eventually became the company's chief operating officer. He left the videogame business behind in 2017 to head up Liverpool FC, but it did not work out: Despite a highly successful run, club ownership did not care for his very public style of leadership, and in 2020 his contract was not renewed.

And he did indeed announce GTA 4 with a tattoo—apologies for the resolution, it was 20 years ago.

In today's message, Moore stated he's "seen this industry reinvent itself time and time again" over those years, and expressed hope that GTA 6 delivers not just commercial success but also "a much-needed shot in the arm (no pun intended…) for the entire ecosystem: developers, publishers, studios, retailers, technology partners and the next generation of creative talent.".

Keep up to date with the most vital stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"The games industry has always been at its best when it dares to dream substantial," Moore concluded.

According to recent reports, moore's upbeat sentiment stands in sharp contrast to that expressed yesterday by game industry legend Warren Spector, who congratulated Rockstar on the launch but mentioned he hopes "GTA 6 is the last of its kind" because it's such an unsustainable draw on resources: "Its billion-dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate. That's especially true when thousands of developers are out of work. A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To pass time and skip ahead in GTA 6 is something that will become more and more of a priority as you progress through the game, with certain quests and activities being tied to certain points in the day or night. That means that if you want to do a night time mission and it's early in the morning, you can either wait for that time to pass, or you can find a way to skip ahead to the moment you need. Below I'll show you how to do that in GTA 6, and the limitations on this system overall.

According to recent reports, to pass time in GTA 6 and skip ahead, the best way to do this is to go to bed. When you lie down and choose to sleep, you also get to pick what time your character wakes up, setting your alarm for morning, noon, evening or night accordingly.

It has been revealed that obviously this means getting back to your home, which for some might easier than others, depending on where you are. You should also make sure that you don't have any time-sensitive missions or activities (marked with an hourglass). If you do, you risk sleeping through them and missing the chance to engage with them. Make sure you check through the GTA 6 index to see if there's anything that's being put at risk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft has confirmed that it's laid off a total of 166 employees across two of its major studios, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec.

Although this figure only accounts for roughly 4% of the publisher's full Canadian workforce, it's obviously still a lot of people to let go of in one fell swoop.

Based on an unnamed source, IGN reports that the layoffs are largely to do with Ubisoft's continued restructuring; it suggests that many of those impacted were working on projects that have since been cancelled.

For context, Montreal has worked on almost every big Ubisoft game you can think of over the past couple of decades. It's right now developing Assassin's Creed Hexe, having spearheaded Assassin's Creed Valhalla and Assassin's Creed Origins previously.

Quebec, meanwhile, has been chiefly responsible for Assassin's Creed Syndicate, Odyssey, and the series' most recent instalment, Shadows.

"As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs," reads an official statement from Ubisoft.

"Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources," it continues.

This console generation has proven tumultuous for Ubisoft as a whole, to the point where its production pipelines have been completely overhauled under Chinese tech giant Tencent's guidance. The manufacturer is still trying to streamline operations more than a year after all of that came into effect.

Naturally, we wish everyone impacted by these layoffs all the best for the future.

[source ign.com, via videogameschronicle.com, gematsu.com].

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite all the outrage and criticism around game developers and publishers using generative AI in gaming, a upcoming report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC) calculates that as many as 40 percent of developers active in the industry use the controversial tools in their work.
  • That's according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from GDC, which gathers data from more than 2,300 respondents including, but not limited to, game industry professionals, made up of developers, producers, marketers, executives, and investors.
  • Recent findings suggest that the report notes that 57 percent of developers who say they do use it, use gen-AI for "text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite all the outrage and criticism around game developers and publishers using generative AI in gaming, a upcoming report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC) calculates that as many as 40 percent of developers active in the industry use the controversial tools in their work. This is up four percent compared to the same report last year.

That's according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from GDC, which gathers data from more than 2,300 respondents including, but not limited to, game industry professionals, made up of developers, producers, marketers, executives, and investors.

Recent findings suggest that the report notes that 57 percent of developers who say they do use it, use gen-AI for "text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations". There appears to be a big split between triple-A studios that use gen-AI (with 27 percent of triple-A developers noting that they "feel encouraged or pressured" to use it) and indie devs, of which only nine percent say the same. Perhaps unsurprisingly - given how vocally against gen-AI a lot of 'frontline developers' have been - the tools are mostly used by "business operations and services, mobile-only studios, and free-to-play developers".

In a recent development, there seems to be a gap in the ages of those willing to use AI tools as well; per the report, over half (54 percent) of people 45 years or older reported using the tools - an eight-point increase from last year's survey. There is also more usage among men (45 percent) than women (33 percent).

What is perhaps more striking is that more people responded to the survey saying that they think AI is having a negative impact on games (55 percent) than responded saying they use the tech, suggesting a trend of caution rather than widespread adoption. Notably, respondents saying they are wary of the technology increased one percent since last year, so more people think AI is having a negative effect on the industry now than at the same time in 2025. Perhaps that's because of the sweeping layoffs we've seen across the games industry, often mentioned in the same breath as AI. Or the 'AI slop' that's been flooding Steam and pushing more traditional developers out. Orr some of the abysmal projects we've seen launch that have clearly used gen-AI assets.

"I did not get into a creative industry to hand over the creativity to an algorithm," remarked one respondent from the UK when explaining why they don't use gen-AI tools. "I got into this industry to collaborate with creative people, not to have an advanced chatbot riff on the ideas of someone who was laid off," said another from California. "I believe that no one should have to read what no human has written and shouldn't have to see what no human has created," said yet another from Minnesota.

The use of generative AI remains controversial in the games industry, though with big companies like Epic and Microsoft doubling down on the tech, it seems this split between developers that want to embrace it and those that don't is only growing larger.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • Industry observers note that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

Industry observers note that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

According to recent reports, spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

You can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

According to recent reports, as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crimson Desert and DokeV developer Pearl Abyss is planning to further integrate generative AI into its workflow.

The South Korean studio stated as much in its latest quarterly Earnings Letter, explaining that it had previously "validated game systems only after implementing them manually." Now, Pearl Abyss is using AI "to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," and argues the move "enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed.".

"However, AI serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity, while the core gameplay experience and actual content creation remain fully driven by our development team," the developer mentioned.

When Crimson Desert first launched, players spotted a crop of suspicious in-game images that looked like they were prompted into existence. Pearl Abyss soon explained that some "2D visual props" were generated with AI tools, but were always intended to be replaced with human-made art, before swiftly patching them out of the hit open-world game.

It seems Pearl Abyss is now even more keen on the controversial tech, however: "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality. AI is being utilized across various stages of development - including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization - and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline. We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously.".

According to recent reports, elsewhere in the letter, the studio noted its previously announced creature-collector DokeV is "targeting a launch in the second half of 2028" and we should hear more about it within the year. DokeV was initially targeting a 2023 launch a few years ago. Meanwhile, Crimson Desert is being prepped for a Nintendo Switch 2 launch "in the first half of next year.".

It has been revealed that the use of generative AI in game development has been a hot topic for years, though it's only become more prevalent in recent months as 'AI slop' floods Steam and substantial companies like Epic Games proudly adopt the tech. A recent report even estimated that around 40 percent of active developers use AI tools in their work.

#17141. Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1512 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • In a recent development, unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

In a recent development, unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a new physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

According to recent reports, on release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

According to recent reports, however, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

The answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Users were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

Industry observers note that in the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

Recent findings suggest that "I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find latest uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

According to recent reports, when looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal consumers: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the matter of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

In a recent development, all the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got significant as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering users.

Industry observers note that "I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Legend of Zelda was in "dire straits" before Breath of the Wild gave the beloved series a massive second wind, according to two former Nintendo marketing leads.

Industry observers note that the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next. Should Zelda lean into its carefully directed history - like the one brilliantly remade in Ocarina of Time - or keep the ball rolling with Breath of the Wild's wide open, spontaneous sandbox?

Nintendo of America's ex-director of social media marketing Kit Ellis and former public relations manager Krysta Yang chimed in on the discourse in their latest podcast (below), and explained that Zelda wasn't doing too hot before the Switch era.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately," Ellis stated in response to fans who reckon "the Zelda team ripped away" series staples, like classic dungeons and linear worlds, at the height of their popularity.

Sources indicate that "I remember, I was going to the focus groups where it was a really dark moment," Ellis continued. "The feedback was like, 'The fan base is dwindling. This is not bringing in newly introduced players.'".

The Legend of Zelda was supposedly "shrinking," while "interest in the audience was getting smaller and smaller" with each fresh entry. "They had to do something dramatic," Ellis said.

Industry observers note that "This series was in dire straits. They were selling, like, nothing," Yang added.

The Zelda series was certainly never irrelevant, but there's a pretty significant gap between the roughly 8m copies Twilight Princess sold at the beginning of the Wii generation, the roughly 3m copies Skyward Sword sold at the end of the console's life, and the 34m copies that Breath of the Wild sold just one console generation later.

According to recent reports, it was a success so major it spawned a wildly ambitious sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, and even influenced the latest 2D Zelda, Echoes of Wisdom. Now that classic Zelda's back in the spotlight, though, I do hope Nintendo's able to slot the series' curated dungeons into whatever the next mainline game becomes.

Queen's Domain's melee combat isn't for everyone: Luckily there's an in-game cheat book you can use to get a gun (and it doesn't bork your achievements cheevos or nothin').

First person King's Field/Metroid Prime-like Queen's Domain has quickly become a top-two shortlister for my personal game of the year, but it can be a prickly, difficult-to-recommend game, particularly in its first 30 minutes or so before you get the game-defining Endu airdash sword.

I'm of a mind with news writer Josh Wolens that the contrast between pre- and post-Endu gameplay really helps sell the game's power curve, but our coworkers Andy Chalk and Morgan Park both bounced off Queen's Domain's admittedly sluggish melee combat.

It has been revealed that there isn't a difficulty selection in Queen's Domain, but there is something close to it: A "witch's grimoire" where you can input codes to receive unique items. Most of these are references to streamers, content creators, or other indie developers.

In a recent development, while referential, they mesh surprisingly well with Queen's Domain's aesthetic, and I don't think they threaten its overall very deliberate sense of progression. What's more, I say playing the game at all is better than avoiding this little cheat code book out of principle.

You can enter the code "hempie" (a reference to the vtuber of the same name) to receive a Soviet SVT-40 semi-automatic battle rifle. A bit incongruous for the medieval fantasy setting, perhaps, but I think it makes for an early game boon while not completely upending Queen's Domain's balance. Most of my preferred later game weapons have been ranged options⁠—the code just gets you one much earlier than you could otherwise. The hempie rifle has already proven an early favorite for Queen's Domain speedrunners like current world record holder Wilbun84, whose video also demonstrates where to find the grimoire.

Industry observers note that on the starting beach, you'll notice a dead tree to your right while facing inland. There is a secret compartment on the other side of the tree, facing away from you: Press the "use" button while close to the tree to reveal the secret compartment (similar to the secret doors scattered throughout Queen's Domain). If you'd like to get even crazier with the grimoire, Destructoid has a full list of all the codes you can input with their corresponding rewards. The grimoire has a limited number of uses, so you can't get everything right away, but you can unlock more uses as the game goes on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
  • Industry observers note that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • Industry observers note that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a newly introduced motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

Industry observers note that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

Industry observers note that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a newly introduced motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

Recent findings suggest that "But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

You know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which right now looks likely to last until at least 2028.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ENHANCEMENT 17TH NOVEMBER: The Blood of Dawnwalker update 1.2 - the update that brings a New Game Plus mode, predominantly - is now available on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X.

New Game Plus, as mentioned below, raises the level cap to 100, and scales enemies and regions in the game around you. Previously, the game was zone-scaled, so some zones were tougher than others. In New Game Plus, this will no longer be the case, so you can go and explore Xanthe's region at the back of Vale Sangora straight away, if you want to.

There'll be new versions of equipment with new stats to find, and they'll be labelled with "NG+" so you know when you've picked one up. You can unlock New Game Plus from the main menu after choosing your base save and difficulty option. All of your accrued skill perks and abilities will be available to you at the start of the Withering Away quest in the game's prologue.

The full patch notes for Dawnwalker upgrade 1.2 are:.

ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER: A Latest Game Plus mode is coming to vampiric RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker next week.

Developer Rebel Wolves has now detailed everything coming with The Blood of Dawnwalker's Update 1.2, currently planned to go live sometime next week, and top of the list of changes is a New Game Plus for players who have already rolled credits on the game.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+," the developer revealed earlier today. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over." Rebel Wolves is upping the level cap to 100 for New Game Plus, which will also have items with updated stats and enemies "balanced and scaled uniformly across all regions.".

Elsewhere in Enhancement 1.2, the studio is making tweaks to "enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat," and improving terrain geometry to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration." We'll need to wait for more comprehensive patch notes before finding out which enemies are getting spongier or flimsier, however.

While the incoming patch doesn't seem to be as beefy as the last - the one that added animal petting and an easier Story mode - it'll be a good way to sink your teeth deeper into a game that's already begging to be replayed, thanks to a time management mechanic that can drastically change any given run.

According to recent reports, the latest game from some former The Witcher 3 veterans came out in September and seems to have been a hit. Eurogamer's The Blood of Dawnwalker review called the game a "familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mainstay of the GTA series has been the presence of sex workers, but Rockstar Games has dropped this aspect for the newly released GTA 6.

As reported by Shack News, unlike most other games in the long-running franchise, you cannot hire a sex worker in GTA 6.

The outlet asked Rockstar about this decision, and received the following response:.

"GTAVI is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run. While we have taken a lot forward from previous GTA titles, everything we have implemented in VI has been done to support the spirit of the story we wanted to tell, and the gameplay systems we wanted to expand upon - things like wanted system, the radio, robberies and car theft. Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTAVI, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story.".

So, in other words, sex workers aren't included this time around because it wouldn't make sense for Jason or Lucia to pursue that, as they're already in a relationship — and that's a substantial part of the story.

As mentioned, they have been present in the series since 2001's GTA 3, and this will be the first 3D game to exclude them.

GTA 6 is also the first game that centres on a couple, however, with the relationship between Jason and Lucia interwoven in the gameplay as well as being a key tenet of the narrative. It seems Rockstar didn't think sex workers would be conducive to this goal.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has stunned players as well as other game developers, with Naughty Dog veteran and Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet world design director praising the game with a mix of disbelief and hyperbole.

"I've made video games for 19 years and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child," Barclay says on Twitter. The Veyron 16.4 can reach 100km/h in 2.5 seconds, Bugatti claims, whereas a Victorian child would obviously need considerable setup time and mechanical assistance – that is, a trebuchet – to even approach such speeds.

Barclay worked on Star Wars: Battlefront 3 at Free Radical Design, The Shoot at Cohort Studios, and also put in years at Crytek and Cloud Imperium Games before joining Naughty Dog in 2016. On his blog, he goes into great depth on the making of The Last of Us Part 2 among many other games and ideas.

"I'm always astonished that their environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting," Barclay states of Rockstar in a separate post. "They do matte style overcast lighting during cloudy days that looks so realistic I just sit and look at the street," he adds.

Recent findings suggest that tim Soret, head of The Last Night developer Odd Tales, agrees with Barclay. "I concur. It truly is alien technology. Hard to comprehend," he states in a post.

In a recent development, GTA 6 is a top-to-bottom marvel. Netflix's long-gestating Magic: The Gathering animated series is called Planeswalker, and it's coming in 2027.

Sources indicate that the title was revealed at MagicCon Atlanta, and Netflix shared a first look at the show on Twitter/X on 13th November. "Every great story begins with a spark. Here's your first look at Planeswalker, a new animated series based on Magic: The Gathering. Coming to Netflix in 2027", the company wrote, and shared a teaser, which you can see below:.

Recent findings suggest that according to a synopsis shared with IGN, the series follows Chandra Nalaar, "a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past". It continues: "Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence".

Netflix first confirmed a Magic: The Gathering series in June 2019, with Avengers: Endgame directors Joe and Anthony Russo attached, and it was originally due in late 2022. Two years in, the original showrunners departed over creative differences, and in September 2024, Netflix confirmed it had started again from scratch with Star Trek: Picard and 12 Monkeys showrunner Terry Matalas in charge.

IGN reports that Matalas, who most recently ran Marvel's VisionQuest, is running the show alongside Cindy Appel. Budapest-based studio DIGIC Pictures is handling the animation.

Lacey Chabert might be the so-called “Queen of Hallmark,” but recently, she proved she has the iconic style of a Disney princess. That's right: the upcoming Hallmark movie, Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True, which is set at Disney World, is such a significant deal that they rolled out a red carpet for the cast, and Chabert did not disappoint with her look for it. In fact, she knocked it out of the park by channeling a beloved Disney Princess for the event.

Industry observers note that the Hallmark darling stepped out in the brand-upcoming Belle-inspired platinum wedding gown from Allure Bridal. The princess gown is decorated with dozens of embroidered roses throughout the strapless scooped bodice and flowing skirt with ornate pickups. Of course, the roses represent the infamous enchanted rose that serves as the ticking time clock for the Beast in the 1991 animated classic.

The rose appliqués are definitely the stars of the dress. Their coral, salmon, and deep red colors pop against the glittery white of the gown. There are also a smattering of smaller blossoms decorated throughout, tying the whole dress together. And the back is just as stunning as the front, with an elegant train featuring the same roses and delicate white buttons down the back of the bodice. It might not be as iconic as the animated film’s yellow gown, but it’s still more than fit for a princess.

Sources indicate that in addition to dazzling the crowd, Chabert also filmed a “get-ready-with-me” video with the official Disney Wedding’s Instagram page, where she shared some of her favorite Christmas memories and revealed that Belle is her favorite princess. So, this look really was a dream for her.

Honestly, the movie premiere and Belle-inspired dress could not have come at a more perfect time, considering Beauty and the Beast is gearing up to celebrate its 35th anniversary on November 22. And just a few days later, on November 28, fans will get to see Chabert's brand latest Disney World Hallmark movie, Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True.

Filmed on Disney World property last year, the movie will follow Lindsey (Chabert) and her extended family as they head to ‘The Most Magical Place on Earth” to celebrate Christmas. However, the magic is short-lived when she discovers that their next-door neighbor is Philip (Travis Van Winkle), a guy she went on a disastrous first date with.

After the awkward reunion, Lindsey decides to make a wish at Cinderella’s wishing well for a love that’s “right out of a fairytale.” She might not think Philip is her Prince Charming, but as their paths continue to cross, they realize they have a lot more in common than their disastrous first date led on.

Latest Update: Star Wars Galactic Racer will get local split-screen multiplayer in early 2027 with new 'Free Play' mode, finally letting racers yell at one another in a tangible space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • Sources indicate that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

Sources indicate that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an glitch for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming update, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Call of Duty Endowment is marking Remembrance Day and its 17th anniversary by encouraging Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone players to pick up its Valor Pack, with all of Activision's net proceeds going towards helping veterans find jobs.

The Call of Duty Endowment Valor Pack - which has been available since Modern Warfare 4 rolled out on 23rd October - was designed by the Endowment and Infinity Ward with US Marine Corps veteran and Medal of Honor recipient Kyle Carpenter in mind.

The items include a melee weapon blueprint inscribed with "Worth Fighting For", plus items called Relentless and Still Standing.

According to the Call of Duty blog, 100 percent of Activision's net proceeds from the pack (after VAT and sales tax) go to the Endowment.

To mark Remembrance Day, players who owned it and launched either game before 6pm GMT on 12th November also received double XP tokens and a DMZ survival kit.

"Veterans bring incredible skills into the workplace after military service," stated Carpenter.

The Endowment, which supports veterans in the UK as well as the US, says it has now helped place more than 180,000 into "high-quality jobs", and wants to reach 200,000 by 2030.

Sources indicate that other partners are also raising money, with Pilot's round-up campaign raising more than £4.7 million ($6 million) for the Endowment since 2019. Polaris will also donate around £19,500 ($25,000) if players collectively complete 5 million rides in its DAGOR vehicle across Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone by 25th November.

Industry observers note that it comes two weeks after Activision apologised to bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it would remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Players discovered that the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died.

Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet recently confirmed it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • Sources indicate that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

Sources indicate that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

According to recent reports, it makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Recent findings suggest that thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

Recent findings suggest that it's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every time the very concept of a GTA 6 has come up in the past eight years, I've had just one wistful opinion to contribute: "I hope they make it more like Red Dead Redemption 2.".

Industry observers note that I'm not a huge GTA guy, but I am a Red Dead head. The sequel is Rockstar's best work (maybe second best now?) because of all the ways it prioritizes roleplay and choice-making by simulating the little things: Mixing tonics, crafting bullets individually, grooming Arthur's mustache. God, I love that stuff.

There was no way Rockstar would repeat all of these life sim-y touches for the louder and faster GTA 6, but I am surprised and elated that my favorite Red Dead 2 feature of them all made the cut: Your car is your horse.

That is to say, Jason and Lucia's personal vehicles are their mobile bases—an essential extension of them. You can't pet or name it, sadly, but it's important to keep track of and take care of your whip, because it's where you keep all your guns and outfits. It's all literally in the trunk: If you want to fetch your shotgun, you have to walk to the back of the car, open it up, and fish it out of a box.

According to recent reports, gone are the days of keeping seven assault rifles, ten SMGs, and four rocket launchers in your back pocket—you can only equip two "long" guns on your back, and large melee weapons like bats have to be stowed away, too. Aside from how cool it is to fish a shotgun out of my trunk like a disgruntled Jason Statham character, the limitation is forcing me to think twice about how to approach missions.

In a recent development, and unlike in Red Dead's lawless towns, the NPCs of Leonida seem to react negatively to the guy walking around with assault rifles on his back. The game tells you early on that police pay closer attention to you when openly carrying firearms—another reason to stow them away when you don't need 'em.

The car trunk is also where extra outfits can be stored. You can bring along five by default (more than Red Dead's saddles allowed), and even this isn't just for vanity. GTA 6's wanted system goes further than police chases: if you lose the cops, your wanted level will linger and cops identify you based on your description, clothes, and your car. The easiest way to go incognito after raising cain is to pull over, pop the trunk, and change outfits.

Keep up to date with the most key stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It's all very smart and cool and I love it. Though I can also understand why others wouldn't—it's a significant break from what GTA has been up to this point. The two gun limit means murderous rampages might end earlier than they used to, and I can foresee getting annoyed the first time I bring a sniper rifle to a shotgun fight and have no way to correct that. But I think this reflects how Rockstar designed GTA 6 to be just as much a life sim as a crime fantasy.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 wants me to constantly make choices and consider what a real human would do. Like in one mission last night, I was left alone without my personal vehicle for the first time. Instead of Rockstar suggesting I grand theft an auto, a tutorial popped for calling a cab. So yea, I took a yellow cab back to my car a few miles away, and it was a chill ride, except for the cabbie who rudely shot down my attempts to make small talk. He's lucky my guns were in my car.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we are now just four days away from the release of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X/S and PS5, but the proximity to the much-anticipated launch date isn't stemming the tide of leaks that has been plaguing the game for much of the past year. Yesterday, a fresh video - seemingly from a record store that received vinyl records of the soundtrack early - showed off the full 34-song tracklist for the game.

Industry observers note that thanks to the listing printed on the back of Grand Theft Auto 6: The Album vinyl, we have a better idea of the licensed music that'll appear in-game. Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson are just some of the names that make up the impressive list. We know about a few of these tracks from September's announcement of the record, but only six tracks were revealed then, not the whole list.

Take a look at the full track listing below:.

You can expect to hear these tracks on the radio - alongside many more, no doubt - and deployed at curated times during cutscenes or in missions, to really tie together the vibe of the city. This is something Vice City did remarkably well its roster of 80s tracks, and I can't wait to see how Rockstar has used more contemporary music in the same way here.

Industry observers note that of course, there have been a lot of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks in the run-up to the game's launch. Another recent example is the full game's map which seemingly leaked online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store. Then there were all the leaks from a group calling itself CyberLeek, which shared unofficial gameplay and map details over the course of a few weeks, before Rockstar had even revealed much gameplay itself.

Amongst all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

It has been revealed that even though it feels like NCIS: Origins just premiered on the 2026 TV schedule, the series is already winding down its third season. Along with a few other CBS shows, Origins’ season was cut short due to scheduling. Instead of a full season, it’s only getting ten episodes and will be replaced by NCIS: Sydney in January, which is also getting just ten episodes. Now, with the Season 3 finale fast approaching, Kyle Schmid is very passionate about getting a Season 4 renewal, but his words don’t exactly reassure me.

Recent findings suggest that the NCIS prequel is only three seasons in, but it’s definitely become a favorite among fans. And with Mark Harmon back as Leroy Jethro Gibbs for all of Season 3, these new episodes are better than ever. And the hope for a fourth season is getting stronger. Unfortunately, there’s no telling when CBS could be making a decision, so Schmid is jumping on the campaign train. The Mike Franks actor told TV Insider just how much the show, crew, and cast deserve another season, and I desperately need it:.

The show is exceptional this year. I’m so proud of the writing team, our cast, our crew, everybody that I had the pleasure of working with for the past four or five months. I think we found our thing this year. I think the show’s found its shape. I think the characters have found their meaning.

As a day one Origins fan, I would love nothing more than to never see this show end, especially because it’s gotten better the longer it’s been on. Even with fewer episodes, Origins has been pumping out some great storylines, and that’s going to continue until the very end of Season 3. Plus, while Schmid couldn’t go into detail about what’s to come, his comments make it clear that Origins cannot end any time soon:.

And let me tell you, when I say I don’t want the show to end like this, the show can’t end like this, and I mean that with all my fucking heart. So when you get to the finale of the show, you will know damn well what I mean when I say it cannot go out like this, so there better be a Season fucking 4.

According to recent reports, this has me very concerned, because Schmid is implying that we're going to be dying to see what happens after Season 3 ends. And let me tell you, I absolutely hate cliffhangers, and I hold grudges against them when demonstrates are canceled right after one, because I know we'll never get a resolution. So, if Origins ends in a way that leaves me ravenous for more, it better not get axed.

Now, I can't say I'm shocked that we probably need to prepare for a brutal cliffhanger. If NCIS: Origins is great at one thing, it’s ending seasons on them. Season 1’s finale saw Lala getting into a car crash, while Season 2 ended with Randy getting abducted. If Season 3 follows the pattern and ends on a cliffhanger, which it sounds like it will, a cancellation would be heartbreaking.

CBS has confirmed that the Season 3 finale of NCIS: Origins will premiere on January 19, so fans will see just what Schmid is talking about in two months. I am also passionate about the show getting another season, and if the finale is as big as it sounds, I will be hopping on the campaign train with the actor.

For now, fans will just have to wait and see what happens. The series is at the moment off for the Thanksgiving holiday, but new episodes will be back on Tuesday, December 1, on CBS, streaming the next day with a Paramount+ subscription.
